import pandas as pd,numpy as np
w=pd.read_parquet('works.parquet');p=pd.read_parquet('passages.parquet')

c='count__domains__DISTANCE_TRAVEL'
w=w.dropna(subset=['year']).drop_duplicates('work_id')
w['r']=w[c]/w.n_passages; w['late']=w.year>=1876
def est(d):
    g=d.groupby(['genre','late']).r.mean().unstack()
    return (g[True]-g[False]).mean(), g

    bs.append(est(s)[0])
print(np.percentile(bs,[2.5,97.5]))
for dc in [['high'],['high','medium']]:
    print(dc,est(w[w.date_confidence.isin(dc)])[0])
x=w[(w.year>=1850)&(w.year<1900)];print('1850-1900',est(x)[0])
print(w.groupby('decade').r.mean())
print(w.groupby(['origin','late']).r.mean().unstack())

Within each of the 8 genres I took the unweighted mean across works, separately for early and late. I then computed the late-minus-early difference per genre and averaged the 8 differences with equal weight. For uncertainty I ran a stratified bootstrap with 4,000 replicates, resampling works within each genre-by-period cell; the CI is the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile. That is not a consistent one-way trend. UK and US subsets show small declines, but most works have unknown origin, so that split cannot be relied on. Alternative explanations for any apparent difference include shifts in genre mix, a few early works per cell, misdated works near the cutoff, noise from coding a single passage per work, and coder inconsistency. Coverage: about 13% of works are pre-1876 (673 works), so early estimates are noisier. The data are adequate to conclude there is no robust shift, and they do not support claiming one. The cited passage IDs are passages coded DISTANCE_TRAVEL, spread across both periods. They only illustrate the construct and do not establish a trend."
